subject: computer-science

moments.title: ENIAC unveiled
moments.who: John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, University of Pennsylvania
moments.body: The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer is unveiled on 14 February 1946. It weighs 30 tons, uses 17,468 vacuum tubes and consumes 150 kW. It was commissioned by the US Army for artillery firing tables. Six women — Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman — were its original programmers, hired as 'computers' (a job title for human calculators).
moments.takeaway: The first general-purpose electronic computer was programmed by women whose names were absent from public coverage for decades.

now.title: Programmers today
now.body: The six ENIAC programmers were inducted into the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame in 1997 — 50 years late. Their story (Kathy Kleiman's research and the 2014 documentary 'The Computers') reshaped popular understanding of computing's origins.
now.open_questions: Why did programming, originally a female-coded job, become male-coded between 1950 and 1990? Mar Hicks' 'Programmed Inequality' (2017) traces the UK's deliberate exclusion of women from computing careers from the 1960s.

reflection: Software was originally seen as clerical work — repetitive, detail-focused, suitable for women — while hardware was 'real' engineering. The status reversal as programming became prestigious tracks the gender flip.
